doc.title: John Lamb interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001

title: Newfoundland and practicing eight to ten hours a day
summary: Posted to Ernest Harmon Air Force Base in Newfoundland, snowed in, he practices relentlessly and reflects that individuals were mostly kind despite the laws.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Newfoundland. Ernest Harmon Air Force Base. That’s where all the military planes used to go through — not all of them but a great deal of them — used to go through during the days when they had props, these four-engine jobs. Elvis Presley came through there and stopped over.

Yeah, and a few others. So I said okay. I went up to the Ernest Harmon Air Force Base and stayed two years, drifts were as high as this ceiling. Eight foot drifts, you know what I mean? And I had a chance to practice. You couldn’t go outside, so I practiced.

Yeah. Now one thing about all three duties, all these duties that I mentioned, Montana, the social life was poor, so I practiced. Three years. Went out and played for a year or so, a couple of years, came back into New Mexico found a teacher and I practiced eight to ten hours a day. Now what could you do? And then I continued this process on and on, remembering that you have a goal to become the world’s greatest bass player. So I practiced, practiced. I’d go and have breakfast, 7 o’clock in the morning, go back as if it were a job, practice until about noon, go back and have lunch, then practice all afternoon unless we had a special rehearsal or we had to play the flag down. Then I might go to the movies for a couple of hours at 6 ‘til about 7:30 or 8, then come back and practice for a couple of hours until about 10 o’clock at night, and then go to the barracks at night, then start the process over the next day. And that’s the way that happened. And Great Falls — did I say Great Falls — Newfoundland was no different. They had social problems up there. They had private clubs. And unless you were a member of the club you couldn’t get in. And you know, no members were black members. So it was sort of like a subtle thing. But one on one, one on one I found that 99 or 98 percent of the people that I’ve met have always been nice people. It’s just that the laws were in such a state that it influenced thinking. And some people had grown up with the mentality that they were in some ways superior because, in some ways. But I knew differently. I still know differently. There is no such thing, it’s just an individual matter, it’s just who you are as a person. And maybe that’s always what I sense about individuals, and somehow whenever they said or did something that was disturbing, somehow it would just sort of go away. It didn’t bother me. I don’t know why.
